lesson.title: Weighing a Mole: Understanding Molar Mass
lesson.summary: Molar mass expresses the mass of one mole of a substance in grams per mole, turning the average atomic masses listed on the periodic table into a practical tool for measuring out chemical amounts.
lesson.body:
Chemists cannot count atoms directly, but they can weigh substances with great precision, so chemistry needed a way to translate between the number of particles in a sample and the mass of that sample. Molar mass is that translation tool. It is defined as the mass of one mole of a substance, expressed in grams per mole, and it is numerically equal to the substance's average atomic mass or, for a compound, the sum of the average atomic masses of every atom in its formula.

The connection to average atomic mass is direct and important. The periodic table lists, for each element, a weighted average of the masses of its naturally occurring isotopes, accounting for how abundant each isotope actually is. Chlorine, for example, exists mostly as two isotopes, roughly 76 percent chlorine-35 with a mass near 34.97 amu and about 24 percent chlorine-37 with a mass near 36.97 amu, and the weighted average of these comes out to 35.45 amu, the value printed on the periodic table. Molar mass simply takes that same number, 35.45, and reassigns its units from atomic mass units per atom to grams per mole. This works because Avogadro's number was defined precisely so that one mole of amu equals one gram, which is why the numerical value carries over unchanged from the atomic scale to the laboratory scale.

For a compound, molar mass is found by adding up the molar masses of every atom in the chemical formula, using the number of each type of atom shown by the subscripts. Water, H2O, has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. Using average atomic masses of 1.008 g/mol for hydrogen and 16.00 g/mol for oxygen, the molar mass of water is 2(1.008) + 16.00 = 18.02 g/mol. A more involved example is calcium carbonate, CaCO3, the main component of limestone and chalk. Adding the molar mass of one calcium atom, 40.08 g/mol, one carbon atom, 12.01 g/mol, and three oxygen atoms, 3 x 16.00 = 48.00 g/mol, gives a total molar mass of 40.08 + 12.01 + 48.00 = 100.09 g/mol.

Molar mass matters because it is the only mole-related quantity that a balance can measure directly. A chemist cannot place a mole on a scale and read it off, but a chemist can weigh out 100.09 grams of calcium carbonate and know, without counting a single particle, that the sample contains exactly one mole, or 6.022 x 10^23 formula units, of CaCO3. This is what makes molar mass the practical partner to Avogadro's number: Avogadro's number defines how many particles are in a mole, and molar mass tells a chemist how much that mole weighs.

Because molar mass sits at the intersection of the mole concept, average atomic mass, and Avogadro's number, it becomes the single most used conversion factor in quantitative chemistry. Every calculation that starts from a measured mass and needs to reach a number of moles, or starts from moles and needs a mass to weigh out, passes through molar mass. Mastering how to build it correctly from a chemical formula is therefore a prerequisite for essentially all of the mole arithmetic that follows.
